introduction: At Thapsacus on the Euphrates, Cyrus at last publicly announces war against the Great King. The troops react to the disclosure and ask for rewards. A clearly separated second scene moves ahead to encouragement shortly before the battle.

Course adaptation of Xenophon, Anabasis 1.4.11–18 and 1.7.3–9. The announced objective, demand for compensation, five-mina promise, continuing pay, crossing, and later encouragement follow the sources. The simplified future speeches are new course wording, not quotations. Promises about wealth and victory are the speakers’ expectations, not the narrator’s guarantees.

Paragraphs 1–4 take place at Thapsacus. Paragraphs 5–7 jump ahead to the pre-battle meeting. Present verbs retell the scenes; future verbs present promises, predictions, and intentions. Irregular futures beyond the regular target are blue-glossed.

reading.translation:
Cyrus and the Greeks come to Thapsacus. The city is beside the Euphrates River. Here Cyrus says openly, “We shall march against the Great King.”

The generals report Cyrus’s statement to the soldiers. They are angry: “Now we learn of the war. We shall not follow without money.” So they request money for the long journey.

Cyrus promises five minas to each soldier at Babylon. “I shall give you money, and I shall provide pay until the arrival back in Ionia.” The soldiers hear the promise.

The Greeks cross the Euphrates. The people of the city marvel at the crossing; the water is not deep. The army now advances, and the war against the King is openly known.

In another place, a short time before the battle, Cyrus summons the generals and captains. He says, “Men of Greece, I honor you and admire your freedom. Now we shall deliberate about the battle.”

“The enemies are numerous and will fight with much shouting. But you will take courage. Upon victory I shall make my friends wealthy and give golden crowns.” In this way Cyrus encourages his listeners.

Some rejoice, while others ask about the promises: “Will Cyrus provide the money? What will each person receive?” The generals urge him not to fight but to remain behind. Victory is not yet certain.

blocks.title: What a promise commits a speaker to
body: ὑπισχνέομαι means promise; ἡ ὑπόσχεσις names a promise. The noun and verb describe different grammatical roles. Cyrus offers μνᾶς and στεφάνους, but describing an offer does not show that it has been fulfilled.

νίκη is victory and βέβαιος is certain or secure. ἡ νίκη οὔπω βεβαία ἐστίν deliberately contrasts present uncertainty with persuasive future wording. ἐπὶ τῇ νίκῃ marks rewards upon success, preserving a condition without assigning subjunctive grammar.

Future forms can belong to very different speech acts: πορευσόμεθα announces an intention, ποιήσω offers a promise, and μαχοῦνται predicts the enemy’s behavior. Use the speaker and context to distinguish them; the ending alone does not certify that a prediction will come true.

sections.title: 1. Sigmatic Futures: Stem, Sigma, and Endings
body: The regular future adds σ to a verb stem and uses primary endings. λύω becomes λύσω, “I shall release”; λυόμεθα becomes λυσόμεθα, “we shall release for ourselves.” There is no augment: future forms are not past-tense forms.

The active endings are -ω, -εις, -ει, -ομεν, -ετε, -ουσι(ν), added after σ. Middle endings are -ομαι, -ῃ/-ει, -εται, -όμεθα, -εσθε, -ονται. In πορευσόμεθα the middle ending identifies first-person plural; the verb’s ordinary meaning is “travel.”

Consonants change before sigma: velars κ, γ, χ combine as ξ; labials π, β, φ as ψ; dentals τ, δ, θ disappear. Thus διώκω → διώξω, γράφω → γράψω, πείθω → πείσω. These are stem changes, not different future person endings.

sections.title: 2. Contract Futures of Verbs in -ίζω
body: Many Attic verbs in -ίζω form an asigmatic contracted future. The present νομίζω gives future νομιῶ, νομιεῖς, νομιεῖ; plural νομιοῦμεν, νομιεῖτε, νομιοῦσι(ν). In the surface form there is no sigma: the stem contracts with future endings in -εω.

Compare νομίζω, “I think,” with νομιῶ, “I shall think.” The present’s ζ disappears and the contracted future has a circumflex in the first-person singular. Forms such as νομιεῖ mark contraction, rather than a sigmatic future with a long vowel before σ.

This is a common Attic pattern, not a promise that every verb ending -ίζω behaves identically in every author. We assess the taught paradigm of νομίζω and its clear examples. Supplementary sentences about thought prepare readers to distinguish expectation from knowledge.

sections.title: 3. Sigmatic Futures of Contract Verbs
body: Present contract verbs normally lengthen their stem vowel before future sigma. τιμάω gives τιμήσω; ποιέω gives ποιήσω; δηλόω gives δηλώσω. These are sigmatic futures even though their present verbs contract.

The pattern differs from the asigmatic contract future νομιῶ. In ποιήσω the η precedes a visible σ; in νομιῶ the future ending is contracted and there is no surface σ. Do not use the single word “contract” to collapse the two systems.

The reading has ἀκολουθήσομεν from ἀκολουθέω and θαρρήσετε from θαρρέω. Read lengthened vowel, sigma, and person ending together. The present τιμῶ contracts α + ω, whereas future τιμήσω retains its clear sigmatic structure.

examples.english: We shall not follow without money.
I shall make my friends wealthy.

checks.prompt: Which is the future of τιμάω?
checks.answer: τιμήσω. α lengthens to η before future σ.

checks.prompt: Which is the future of ποιέω?

sections.title: 4. Deponents and Futures with Middle Form
body: A future can have middle endings and an active English meaning. πορεύομαι → πορεύσομαι, “I shall travel”; βουλεύομαι → βουλεύσομαι, “I shall deliberate.” These verbs already have middle forms in the present. Learn the future with the dictionary entry.

Other familiar verbs change to middle form in the future: ἀκούω → ἀκούσομαι, “I shall hear”; λαμβάνω → λήψομαι, “I shall receive.” Their middle endings do not make them English passives. The future stem of λαμβάνω is irregular and is supplied rather than guessed from the present.

μάχομαι has the contracted middle future μαχοῦμαι, “I shall fight,” with μαχεῖται, “he will fight,” and μαχοῦνται, “they will fight.” Recognize this reading form as supported vocabulary. For all these verbs person comes from the ending and lexical meaning from the verb.

sections.title: 5. Prediction, Intention, and Promise
body: A future indicative places an action in expectation, but its practical force depends on context. πορευσόμεθα announces what Cyrus intends the expedition to do. ποιήσω promises what he undertakes to provide. μαχοῦνται predicts what the enemies will do.

Compare present and future: νῦν ἀκούομεν, “now we hear”; ἀκουσόμεθα, “we shall hear.” A future may be questioned or denied: ἆρα παρέξει; “will he provide?” οὐκ ἀκολουθήσομεν, “we shall not follow.” The future remains future inside a question or negative statement.

Separate the speaker’s commitment from a narrator’s account of events. Cyrus’s rewards depend on success, and the reading has not yet described the battle. A grammatically confident future does not provide evidence that the money, return, or victory will actually occur.

examples.english: We hear now; we shall hear tomorrow (supplementary example).

checks.prompt: What kind of statement is Cyrus’s “I shall make my friends wealthy”?
checks.answer: promise. The speaker undertakes to reward his friends.

checks.prompt: What kind is “The enemies will fight”?
checks.answer: prediction. It predicts another group’s conduct.

sections.title: Disclosure at Thapsacus
body: At Anabasis 1.4.11 Cyrus tells the Greek commanders that the march is against the Great King and asks them to relay it. The soldiers are angry with their generals and say that they had known the objective but concealed it. Xenophon reports their accusation; the course does not convert that accusation into proof of what every commander knew.

The soldiers demand an offer comparable to what they expected from earlier service. Cyrus promises five minas of silver to each upon reaching Babylon and full pay until he brings the Greeks back to Ionia. They accept and cross. The chronological contrast with Tarsus is essential: suspicion there becomes explicit disclosure here.

sections.title: Crossing and reported interpretation
body: Xenophon says the Euphrates can be forded at this crossing. The people of Thapsacus report that previously it had not been passable on foot and interpret its apparent submission to Cyrus as a sign that he should rule. These are the inhabitants’ reported words and interpretation, not a verified miracle or a hydrological rule for every year.

The adapted Greek retains the shallow water and their astonishment while omitting complex supernatural claims. Crossing the river changes the army’s practical situation, but the reading does not yet give the outcome of the royal contest. A source can record what people regard as a sign without endorsing that sign as a guarantee.

sections.title: Persuasion shortly before the battle
body: The second source scene, Anabasis 1.7.3–9, takes place later, near the approaching battle. Cyrus praises the Greeks and their freedom, describes the enemies’ numbers and noise, and offers rewards. His comparative claims about peoples are persuasive claims by a commander, not objective rankings of human worth.

Gaulites reports doubts about whether Cyrus will remember or be able to fulfill his offers. Cyrus answers with the resources of the empire and promises golden crowns; those speaking with him also urge him to avoid fighting personally and to remain behind them. The army’s encouragement coexists with uncertainty about the patron and his choices.
